\label{thm:main1}
Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_N\) be i.i.d. copies of a centered sub-Gaussian random
vector \(X\in\mathbb R^d\) with covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) and
sub-Gaussian constant \(K\). Let \(p\ge 2\) be an integer. Then, for every
\(q\ge1\),
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}
\bigg\|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{\otimes p}
-
\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf F}^q
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\lesssim_p
K^p
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N}
+
\rho_p(\Sigma)\sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright),
\]
where
\[
\rho_p(\Sigma)
:=
\begin{cases}
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2},
& p \text{ even},\\[3pt]
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-1)/2}\|\Sigma\|^{1/2},
& p \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover, if $X$ is Gaussian, then
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\mathbb{E} \bigg\|
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^N
X_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf{F}}^q\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\asymp_p
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}}{\sqrt{N}}
+
\rho_{p,G}(\Sigma)\sqrt{\frac{q}{N}}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N},
\]
where
\[
\rho_{p,G}(\Sigma)
:=
\begin{cases}
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{p/2-1}\|\Sigma\|, & p \text{ even},\\[3pt]
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{(p-1)/2}\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}, & p \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

Then, for every \(qge1\), \[ mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( E bigg\| frac1Nsum_i=1^N X_i^otimes p - E X^otimes p bigg\|_mathsf F^q aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/q lesssim_p K^p mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( fracTr(Sigma)^p/2sqrt N + rho_p(Sigma)sqrtfracqland NN + \|Sigma\|^p/2fracq^p/2N aftergroupegrouporiginalright), \] where \[ rho_p(Sigma) := \|Sigma\|_mathsf F^p/2, & p even,\\[3pt] \|Sigma\|_mathsf F^(p-1)/2\|Sigma\|^1/2, & p odd. \] Moreover, if X is Gaussian, then \[ mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft(E bigg\| frac1N sum_i=1^N X_i^otimes p-E X^otimes p bigg\|_F^qaftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/q asymp_p fracTr(Sigma)^p/2sqrtN + rho_p,G(Sigma)sqrtfracqN + \|Sigma\|^p/2fracq^p/2N, \] where \[ rho_p,G(Sigma) := \|Sigma\|_F^p/2-1\|Sigma\|, & p even,\\[3pt] \|Sigma\|_F^(p-1)/2\|Sigma\|^1/2, & p odd. \]

\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item
The first upper bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:main1} is sharp over the class
of sub-Gaussian distributions. More precisely, in
Example~\ref{example:subgaussian_tensor_sharpness} we construct a centered
random vector \(X\) with covariance \(\Sigma\) and sub-Gaussian constant
\(K\asymp1\) such that, for every integer \(p\ge2\), every \(q\ge1\), and
i.i.d. copies \(X_1,\ldots,X_N\) of \(X\),
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E} \bigg\|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf F}^q
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\gtrsim_p
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N}
+
\rho_p(\Sigma)\sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N},
\]
where \(\rho_p(\Sigma)\) is defined in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main1}. Hence all three terms in the upper bound are
necessary, up to constants depending only on \(p\).



\item 
It is instructive to compare the sub-Gaussian and Gaussian bounds. The trace
and large-deviation scales coincide in the two settings. When \(p\) is odd,
the intermediate scales also coincide:
\[
\rho_p(\Sigma)
=
\rho_{p,G}(\Sigma)
=
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-1)/2}\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}.
\]
By contrast, when \(p\) is even,
\[
\rho_p(\Sigma)=\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2},
\qquad
\rho_{p,G}(\Sigma)
=
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2-1}\|\Sigma\|.
\]
Thus, at even orders, passing from the Gaussian distribution to the full
sub-Gaussian class may enlarge the covariance-dependent coefficient in the intermediate scale by the factor
$
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F} /\|\Sigma\|,
$
which can be as large as
\(\sqrt{\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)}\). This enlargement is intrinsic, as illustrated by
Example~\ref{example:subgaussian_tensor_sharpness}; the parity effect is discussed further in Subsection \ref{subsec:sharpness}. 

\item Taking \(q=u\) in Theorem~\ref{thm:main1} and applying Markov's inequality
yields that, for every \(u\ge1\), with probability at least \(1-e^{-u}\),
\[
\bigg\|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf F}
\lesssim_p
K^p
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N}
+
\rho_p(\Sigma)\sqrt{\frac{u\land N}{N}}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\frac{u^{p/2}}N
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright).
\]
If \(X\) is Gaussian,  with probability at least \(1-e^{-u}\),
\[
\bigg\|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf F}
\lesssim_p
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N}
+
\rho_{p,G}(\Sigma)\sqrt{\frac{u}{N}}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\frac{u^{p/2}}{N}.
\]
\end{enumerate}

\label{rem:ULC-third-moment}
In a very recent work, Chen and Klartag determine the optimal universal constant in the
thin-shell inequality \cite{chen2026thinshell}.  Their Theorem 1.2  shows that every isotropic
log-concave random vector \(Y\in\mathbb R^d\) satisfies the sharp estimate
\[
\bigl\|\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes 3}\bigr\|_{\mathsf F}^{2}
\le 4d.
\]
Equality is attained when the coordinates of $Y$ are independent standard, centered, exponential random variables. Thus, at order \(p=3\), a sharp estimate is available under mere
log-concavity in the isotropic setting. By contrast, under the stronger
assumption of uniform log-concavity,
Proposition~\ref{prop:ULC-moment-tensors} provides anisotropic bounds at
all orders needed for the structured martingale coupling argument in the
proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main2}. It would be interesting to investigate
sharp dimension-free, covariance-dependent Frobenius-norm bounds for
higher-order moment tensors under mere log-concavity.

\label{lem:Hilbert-moment-reduction}
Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\) be independent centered random vectors in a real
Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), let \(q\ge2\), and assume that
\[
\|Z_i\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}
:=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}\|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^q
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
<\infty,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.
\]
Then
\[
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i
\bigg\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}
\asymp
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N \|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}
+
\sup_{\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\sum_{i=1}^N
\langle h,Z_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_{q/2}}.
\]

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main1}
nodes.statement: We first consider \(qge2\). Applying Lemma~ in \((mathbb R^d)^otimes p\), equipped with the Frobenius inner product, to the independent centered tensors \[ X_i^otimes p-E X^otimes p, i=1,ldots,N, \] and then dividing the resulting equivalence by \(N\), we obtain mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( E bigg\| frac1Nsum_i=1^N mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( X_i^otimes p-E X^otimes p aftergroupegrouporiginalright) bigg\|_mathsf F^q aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/q & asymp frac1N mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| bigg( sum_i=1^N big\| X_i^otimes p-E X^otimes p big\|_mathsf F^2 bigg)^1/2 aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_qnonumber\\ & + frac1N sup_\|A\|_mathsf Fle1 bigg\| sum_i=1^N mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleftlangle A, X_i^otimes p-E X^otimes p aftergroupegrouporiginalrightrangle_mathsf F bigg\|_L_q/2. In applying Proposition~ below, replacing \(q/2\) by \(q\) on its right-hand side changes the estimates only by constants depending on \(p\). noindentSub-Gaussian case. Combining with the sub-Gaussian parts of Propositions~ and~ proves the asserted bound directly when \(p\) is even. When \(pge3\) is odd, the same estimates give the asserted bound except that rho_p(Sigma)sqrtfracqland NN is replaced by rho_p(Sigma)sqrtfrac qN. If \(qle N\), these quantities coincide. If \(q>N\), then \[ rho_p(Sigma)^2 le Tr(Sigma)^p/2\|Sigma\|^p/2, Nqlesqrt N\,q^p/2, \] where we used \(\|Sigma\|_mathsf F^2leTr(Sigma)\|Sigma\|\), \(\|Sigma\|leTr(Sigma)\), and \(pge3\). Consequently, rho_p(Sigma)sqrtfrac qN le mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( fracTr(Sigma)^p/2sqrt N aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/2 mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( frac\|Sigma\|^p/2q^p/2N aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/2le frac12 mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( fracTr(Sigma)^p/2sqrt N + frac\|Sigma\|^p/2q^p/2N aftergroupegrouporiginalright). Thus the untruncated term is absorbed by the trace and large-deviation terms when \(q>N\). We therefore obtain mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( E bigg\| frac1Nsum_i=1^N X_i^otimes p -E X^otimes p bigg\|_mathsf F^q aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/q lesssim_p K^p mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( fracTr(Sigma)^p/2sqrt N + rho_p(Sigma)sqrtfracqland NN + frac\|Sigma\|^p/2q^p/2N aftergroupegrouporiginalright). noindentGaussian case. \medskip
\noindent\textbf{Sub-Gaussian upper bound.}
\medskip

For \(i=1,\ldots,N\), set
\[
W_i
:=
\big\|
X_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}
\big\|_{\mathsf F}^2.
\]
Then, for \(q\ge2\),
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N
\big\|
X_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}
\big\|_{\mathsf F}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}
=
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N W_i
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}^{1/2}.

\cite[Theorem~2.1 and Remark~2.2]{hsu2012tail}, see also
\cite[Lemma~2.7 and Remark~2.8]{zhivotovskiy2024dimension}, implies that,
for every \(t>0\), with probability at least \(1-e^{-t}\),
\[
\|X\|_2
\lesssim
K
\sqrt{
\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)+t\|\Sigma\|
}.
\]

\begin{equation*}\label{eq:subg-Euclidean-moment}
\|\|X\|_2\|_{L_s}
\lesssim
K
\sqrt{
\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)+s\|\Sigma\|
},
\qquad s\ge1.
\end{equation*}

\(\|x^{\otimes p}\|_{\mathsf F}=\|x\|_2^p\), the triangle inequality and Jensen's inequality give
\[
\big\|
X^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}

\le
\|X\|_2^p+\mathbb{E}\|X\|_2^p.
\]

=

\big\|
X_1^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}

\bigg\|_{L_r}

\medskip
\noindent \textbf{Gaussian upper bound.}
\medskip

When \(X\) is Gaussian, the upper bound follows immediately from the sub-Gaussian estimate above, since a centered Gaussian random vector satisfies \eqref{eq:def-subg} with \(K=\sqrt{8/3}\).

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Gaussian lower bound.}
\medskip

Suppose now that \(X=G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)\). We first treat \(q\ge2\) and set
\(r:=q/2\ge1\).

\medskip
\textbf{Step 1: a lower bound for \(\|W_1\|_{L_s}\).} We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gaussian-W1-lower}
\|W_1\|_{L_s}
\gtrsim_p
\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^p+s^p\|\Sigma\|^p,
\qquad s\ge1.
\end{equation}
Since
\[
\|W_1\|_{L_s}
=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\big\|G^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_{2s}}^2,
\]
it suffices to bound the latter norm below by
\(\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}\) and by \(s^{p/2}\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\) separately.

Let \(v_1\) be a unit top eigenvector of \(\Sigma\) and set
\(\xi_1:=\|\Sigma\|^{-1/2}\langle G,v_1\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). Testing
against \(A:=v_1^{\otimes p}\), which satisfies \(\|A\|_{\mathsf F}=1\),
gives
\[
\big\|G^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}
\ge
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft|
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle A,G^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright|
=
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft|\xi_1^p-\mathbb{E}\xi_1^p\aftergroup\egroup\originalright|.
\]
Since \(\|\xi_1^p-\mathbb{E}\xi_1^p\|_{L_{2s}}\asymp_p s^{p/2}\) for \(s\ge1\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gaussian-W1-tail-scale}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\big\|G^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_{2s}}
\gtrsim_p
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}s^{p/2}.
\end{equation}

For the trace scale, recall that by Wick's formula \(\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}=0\)
when \(p\) is odd, while for \(p\) even \(\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\) is a sum of
\((p-1)!!\) tensors, each obtained by permuting the legs of
\(\Sigma^{\otimes p/2}\) and therefore of Frobenius norm
\(\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2}\). Hence, with \(b_p:=(p-1)!!\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gaussian-mean-tensor-upper}
\big\|\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}
\le
b_p\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2}.
\end{equation}
Since \(\|x^{\otimes p}\|_{\mathsf F}=\|x\|_2^p\), orthogonality of the
mean and the fluctuation in \((\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes p}\) together with
Jensen's inequality gives
\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}\big\|G^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}^2
&=
\mathbb{E}\|G\|_2^{2p}
-
\big\|\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}^2\nonumber\\
&\ge
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_2^2\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^p
-
b_p^2\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^p
=
\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^p-b_p^2\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^p.
\label{eq:gaussian-W1-L2-identity}
\end{align}
By \(\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^2\le\|\Sigma\|\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)\),
\[
b_p^2\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^p
\le
b_p^2
\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^p
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\frac{\|\Sigma\|}{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{p/2}.
\]
Set \(\kappa_p:=(2b_p^2)^{2/p}\). If \(\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)\ge\kappa_p\|\Sigma\|\),
the right-hand side is at most \(\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^p\), so
\eqref{eq:gaussian-W1-L2-identity} and \(2s\ge2\) yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gaussian-W1-trace-scale}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\big\|G^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_{2s}}
\ge
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\big\|G^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_2}
\ge
2^{-1/2}\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}.
\end{equation}
If instead \(\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)<\kappa_p\|\Sigma\|\), then, since \(s\ge1\),
\[
\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}
\le
\kappa_p^{p/2}\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}
\le
\kappa_p^{p/2}s^{p/2}\|\Sigma\|^{p/2},
\]
so the trace scale is already controlled by
\eqref{eq:gaussian-W1-tail-scale}. In either case, combining
\eqref{eq:gaussian-W1-tail-scale} and
\eqref{eq:gaussian-W1-trace-scale} and squaring proves
\eqref{eq:gaussian-W1-lower}.


\medskip
\textbf{Step 2: the two-sided Latała's estimate.} We use
\eqref{eq:Latala-square-function}, which is an equivalence, and bound the
supremum from below by evaluating it at two admissible values of \(s\).

Take first \(s:=\max\{1,r/N\}\). If \(r\le N\), then \(s=1\) and the
corresponding term equals \(N\|W_1\|_{L_1}\). If \(r>N\), then
\(s=r/N\) and the corresponding term equals
\[
N\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\frac Nr\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{N/r}\|W_1\|_{L_{r/N}}
\ge
e^{-1/e}N\|W_1\|_{L_1},
\]

\[

\ge
e^{-1/e}\|W_1\|_{L_r}
\gtrsim_p
r^p\|\Sigma\|^p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^N W_i\bigg\|_{L_r}
\gtrsim_p
N\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^p+r^p\|\Sigma\|^p,
\]

\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N
\big\|G_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}
\gtrsim_p
\sqrt N\,\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}q^{p/2}.

\[
V:=
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N
\big\|G_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\big\|_{\mathsf F}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
=
\big\|
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(G_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)_{i=1}^N
\big\|_{\ell_2^N((\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes p})},
\]
and that
\(\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(G_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)_{i=1}^N\) is a
Hilbert-space-valued Gaussian chaos of order at most \(p\) in the
Gaussian vector \((G_1,\ldots,G_N)\). Finite-chaos moment comparison
\cite[Theorem~5.10]{Janson1997GaussianHilbertSpaces} therefore gives
\[
\|V\|_{L_2}
\lesssim_p
\|V\|_{L_1}
\le
\|V\|_{L_q}.
\]
Since the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:master-diagonal-g} at \(q=2\) is
comparable, up to constants depending only on \(p\), to its value at
\(q\in[1,2)\), the lower bound extends to \(1\le q<2\). This completes
the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:master-scalar-projections}
nodes.statement: Throughout the proof, set \[ Z_i:=X_i^otimes p-E X^otimes p, i=1,ldots,N, Z:=X^otimes p-E X^otimes p. \] We first consider \(qge2\). For \(alphage0\), define \[ mathcal L_alpha(N,q) := sup_max\2,q/N\le sle q frac qs mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( frac Nq aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/s s^alpha . \] An elementary optimization gives mathcal L_0(N,q) asymp sqrtN(qland N), mathcal L_1/2(N,q) asymp sqrtNq, and, for every \(alphage1\), mathcal L_alpha(N,q) asymp_alpha sqrtNq+q^alpha . We shall also use the fact that, for nonnegative \(f_s\) and \(g_s\), sup_s(f_s+g_s)asympsup_s f_s+sup_s g_s. noindentSub-Gaussian upper bound. Recall that \[ rho_p(Sigma) = \|Sigma\|_mathsf F^p/2, & p even,\\[3pt] \|Sigma\|_mathsf F^(p-1)/2\|Sigma\|^1/2, & p odd. \] By Lemma~, followed by interchanging the suprema over \(A\) and \(s\), we have sup_\|A\|_mathsf F=1 mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| sum_i=1^N langle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q &asymp sup_max\2,q/N\le sle q fracqs mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft(fracNqaftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/s sup_\|A\|_mathsf F=1 mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| langle A,Zrangle_mathsf F aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_s. Applying the sub-Gaussian bound in Lemma~ and , we therefore obtain sup_\|A\|_mathsf F=1 mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| sum_i=1^N langle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q lesssim_p K^p rho_p(Sigma)mathcal L_0(N,q) + \|Sigma\|^p/2mathcal L_p/2(N,q), & p even,\\[3pt] rho_p(Sigma)mathcal L_1/2(N,q) + \|Sigma\|^p/2mathcal L_p/2(N,q), & p odd. Since \(\|Sigma\|^p/2lerho_p(Sigma)\), and imply sup_\|A\|_mathsf F=1 bigg\| sum_i=1^Nlangle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F bigg\|_L_q lesssim_p K^p rho_p(Sigma)sqrtN(qland N) + \|Sigma\|^p/2q^p/2, & p even,\\[3pt] rho_p(Sigma)sqrtNq + \|Sigma\|^p/2q^p/2, & p odd. Indeed, the additional term \(\|Sigma\|^p/2sqrtNq\) arising from is absorbed as follows. When \(p\) is even, it is absorbed by the first term if \(qle N\), and by \(\|Sigma\|^p/2q^p/2\) if \(q>N\). When \(p\) is odd, it is absorbed by \(rho_p(Sigma)sqrtNq\). noindentGaussian two-sided bound. Suppose now that \(X\) is Gaussian. Repeating the preceding argument with the Gaussian two-sided estimate in Lemma~, we obtain sup_\|A\|_mathsf F=1 bigg\| sum_i=1^Nlangle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F bigg\|_L_q asymp_p rho_p,G(Sigma)mathcal L_1(N,q) + \|Sigma\|^p/2mathcal L_p/2(N,q), & p even,\\[3pt] rho_p,G(Sigma)mathcal L_1/2(N,q) + \|Sigma\|^p/2mathcal L_p/2(N,q), & p odd, where \[ rho_p,G(Sigma) = \|Sigma\|_F^p/2-1\|Sigma\|, & p even,\\[3pt] \|Sigma\|_F^(p-1)/2\|Sigma\|^1/2, & p odd. \] Since \(\|Sigma\|^p/2lerho_p,G(Sigma)\), and give sup_\|A\|_mathsf F=1 bigg\| sum_i=1^Nlangle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F bigg\|_L_q asymp_p rho_p,G(Sigma)mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft(sqrtNq+qaftergroupegrouporiginalright) + \|Sigma\|^p/2q^p/2, & p even,\\[3pt] rho_p,G(Sigma)sqrtNq + \|Sigma\|^p/2q^p/2, & p odd. It remains to consider \(1le q<2\). The sub-Gaussian and Gaussian upper bounds follow from moment monotonicity and the corresponding estimates at \(q=2\), since their right-hand sides at \(q=2\) are bounded, up to constants depending only on \(p\), by those at \(q\). For the Gaussian lower bound, for every \(A\), the random variable \(sum_i=1^N langle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(p\) in Gaussian random variables. The finite-chaos moment comparison therefore gives \[ bigg\| sum_i=1^N langle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F bigg\|_L_2 lesssim_p bigg\| sum_i=1^N langle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F bigg\|_L_1 le bigg\| sum_i=1^N langle A,Z_irangle_mathsf F bigg\|_L_q. \] Taking the supremum over \(\|A\|_mathsf F=1\), applying the Gaussian lower bound at \(q=2\), and comparing its right-hand side with that at \(q\) proves the desired lower bound for \(1le q<2\). This completes the proof.

\label{example:subgaussian_tensor_sharpness}
Fix an integer \(p\ge2\). Let
\[
\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d>0,
\qquad
\Lambda:=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d),
\qquad
\lambda_1=\|\Lambda\|.
\]
Let \(G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda)\), let
\(\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^d\) have independent Rademacher entries, and let
\(R\), independent of \(G\) and \(\varepsilon\), take the values \(0\) and
\(\sqrt2\), each with probability \(1/2\). Define
\[
Y:=R\Lambda^{1/2}\varepsilon,
\qquad
X:=(G,Y)\in\mathbb R^{2d}.
\]
Standard Gaussian and Rademacher sub-Gaussian estimates, together with the
boundedness of \(R\), show that \(X\) satisfies \eqref{eq:def-subg} with
\(K\asymp1\). Since \(\mathbb{E} R^2=1\), \(X\) is centered and has covariance matrix
\[
\Sigma
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\Lambda&0\\
0&\Lambda
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:subgaussian_tensor_covariance_relation}
\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)=2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda),
\qquad
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}=\sqrt2 \|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F},
\qquad
\|\Sigma\|=\|\Lambda\|.
\end{equation}


For \(i=1,\ldots,N\), let \((G_i,R_i,\varepsilon_i)\) be independent
copies of \((G,R,\varepsilon)\), and set
\[
Y_i:=R_i\Lambda^{1/2}\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
X_i:=(G_i,Y_i).
\]
Then \(X_1,\ldots,X_N\) are i.i.d. with the same distribution as \(X\). Let
\[
S_p
:=
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} X^{\otimes p}.
\]
We show that, for every \(q\ge1\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:subgaussian_tensor_sharpness}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\mathbb{E}\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}^q\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\gtrsim_p
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N}
+
\rho_p(\Sigma)\sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N},
\end{equation}
where \(\rho_p(\Sigma)\) is defined in Theorem \ref{thm:main1}.

Restricting \(S_p\) to the tensor block corresponding entirely to the
\(G\)-coordinates, we obtain
\[
\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}
\ge
\bigg\|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N G_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} G^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf F}.
\]
The Gaussian lower bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:main1} therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_lower}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\mathbb{E}\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}^q\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\gtrsim_p
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N}
+
\rho_{p,G}(\Lambda)\sqrt{\frac qN}
+
\|\Lambda\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N}.
\end{equation}

Suppose first that \(p\) is odd. In this case,
\[
\rho_{p,G}(\Lambda)
=
\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-1)/2}\|\Lambda\|^{1/2}
=
\rho_p(\Lambda).
\]
Moreover, $\sqrt{\frac qN}
\ge
\sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}}$.
Thus \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_sharpness} follows from
\eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_lower} and
\eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_covariance_relation}.

Now suppose that \(p=2k\) is even. Retaining the first and third terms in
\eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_lower}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_scales}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\mathbb{E}\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}^q\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\gtrsim_p
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N}
+
\|\Lambda\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N}.
\end{equation}
It remains to obtain the intermediate fluctuation scale lower bound. Set
\[
B:=\frac{\Lambda}{\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}},
\qquad
A:=B^{\otimes k}.
\]
Then
\[
\|A\|_{\mathsf F}
=
\|B\|_{\mathsf F}^k
=
1.
\]
Since $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p}$
is the tensor block of \(S_p\) corresponding entirely to the
\(Y\)-coordinates, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:subgaussian_tensor_block_test}
\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}
\ge
\bigg\|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf F}
\ge
\bigg|
\bigg\langle
A,
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p}
\bigg\rangle_{\mathsf F}
\bigg|.
\end{equation}

Since \(Y=R\Lambda^{1/2}\varepsilon\) and every coordinate of \(\varepsilon\) takes values in \(\{\pm 1\}\),
\[
Y^\top B Y
=
\frac{R^2}{\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}}
\varepsilon^\top\Lambda^2\varepsilon
=
\frac{R^2}{\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}}
\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j^2
=
R^2\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}.
\]
Consequently, recalling that \(p=2k\),
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle A,Y^{\otimes p}\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}
=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle B^{\otimes k},Y^{\otimes 2k}\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}
=
(Y^\top B Y)^k
=
R^{2k}\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^k.
\]
For \( i = 1, \ldots, N\), define the Rademacher random variable \(\eta_i\) by 
\[
R_i^{2k}-\mathbb{E} R^{2k}
=
2^{k-1}\eta_i.
\]
Then \(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_N\) are independent, and
\[
\bigg\langle
A,
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p}
\bigg\rangle_{\mathsf F}
=
2^{k-1}\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^k
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\eta_i.
\]
Combining this identity with
\eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_block_test} and taking \(L_q\)-norms, we obtain
\begin{align}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\mathbb{E}\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}^q\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\ge
2^{k-1}\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^k
\bigg\|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\eta_i
\bigg\|_{L_q}
\asymp_p
\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2}
\sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}},
\label{eq:subgaussian_tensor_middle_even}
\end{align}
where the last step follows from the two-sided moment estimate for
Rademacher sums
\cite{montgomerysmith1990rademacher}.
Combining \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_scales} and
\eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_middle_even}, and using
\eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_covariance_relation}, proves
\eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_sharpness} in the even case.

For every \(vinker(Sigma)\), convex domination applied to \(xmapsto|langle v,xrangle|\) gives \[ E|langle v,Zrangle| le E|langle v,G_Sigmarangle| = 0. \] Thus \(Zin E\) almost surely. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:Hilbert-Gaussian-tensor-Lq}
nodes.statement: By orthogonal invariance, we may assume that \[ Sigma = diag(lambda_1,ldots,lambda_d), G_Sigma = mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( lambda_1^1/2xi_1,ldots,lambda_d^1/2xi_d aftergroupegrouporiginalright), \] where \(xi_1,ldots,xi_d\) are independent standard Gaussian random variables; indeed, an orthogonal change of coordinates can be absorbed into \(T\) without changing its Frobenius norm. In these coordinates, \(\|Sigma\|=max_1le ile dlambda_i\) and \(\|Sigma\|_mathsf F^2=sum_i=1^dlambda_i^2\). Since symmetrizing \(T\) does not change \(T(G_Sigma,ldots,G_Sigma)\) and cannot increase \(\|T\|_mathsf F\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(T\) is symmetric. Writing \(T_i_1,ldots,i_p:=T(e_i_1,ldots,e_i_p)inmathcal H\), we have T(G_Sigma,ldots,G_Sigma) = sum_i_1,ldots,i_p=1^d lambda_i_1^1/2cdotslambda_i_p^1/2 T_i_1,ldots,i_p xi_i_1cdotsxi_i_p. noindentStep 1: Chaos decomposition. Let \(H_r\) denote the probabilists' Hermite polynomial of degree \(r\). For an ordered \(j\)-tuple \(mathbf k=(k_1,ldots,k_j)in\1,ldots,d\^j\), define \[ nu_ell(mathbf k) := bigl|\r:k_r=ell\bigr|, H_mathbf k(xi) := prod_ell=1^d H_nu_ell(mathbf k)(xi_ell), \] with the convention \(H_varnothing=1\). Since \(sum_ell=1^dnu_ell(mathbf k)=j\), the multivariate Hermite polynomial \(H_mathbf k(xi)\) has total Hermite degree \(j\) and hence belongs to the \(j\)-th homogeneous Gaussian chaos. When \(jge1\), it is also centered. Indeed, at least one of the multiplicities \(nu_ell(mathbf k)\) is positive, so independence, together with \(E H_m(xi_ell)=0\) for \(mge1\), yields \(E H_mathbf k(xi)=0\). For \(0le alelfloor p/2rfloor\), let \(mathcal P_a(p)\) be the collection of all choices of \(a\) disjoint pairs of positions in \(\1,ldots,p\\), and let \(V(pi)\) denote the set of positions covered by \(piinmathcal P_a(p)\). The Wick expansion in coordinates reads xi_i_1cdotsxi_i_p = sum_a=0^lfloor p/2rfloor sum_piinmathcal P_a(p) bigg( prod_\r,s\inpi mathbf 1_\i_r=i_s\ bigg) H_(i_t)_tnotin V(pi)(xi), where each pair identifies two coordinate indices, while the remaining \(p-2a\) indices form a Hermite polynomial of total degree \(p-2a\). Fix \(a\) and set \(j:=p-2a\). Substituting into , the pairs contract \(T\) against \(a\) copies of \(Sigma\), which leads us to define \[ B^(a)_k_1,ldots,k_j := sum_r_1,ldots,r_a=1^d lambda_r_1cdotslambda_r_a T_r_1,r_1,ldots,r_a,r_a,k_1,ldots,k_j, \] so that \(B^(0)_k_1,ldots,k_p=T_k_1,ldots,k_p\). Since \(T\) is symmetric, all pairings in \(mathcal P_a(p)\) give the same contribution, and \(|mathcal P_a(p)|=p!/(2^aa!j!)\). Consequently, setting \[ Y_j := fracp!2^aa!j! sum_k_1,ldots,k_j=1^d lambda_k_1^1/2cdotslambda_k_j^1/2 B^(a)_k_1,ldots,k_j H_(k_1,ldots,k_j)(xi), \] we obtain the chaos decomposition T(G_Sigma,ldots,G_Sigma) = sum_substack0le jle p\jequiv p\!\!\!pmod2 Y_j, where each \(Y_j\) is an \(mathcal H\)-valued random variable in the \(j\)-th Gaussian chaos generated by \(xi_1,ldots,xi_d\). More precisely, for every \(uinmathcal H\), the scalar random variable \(langle Y_j,urangle_mathcal H\) is a linear combination of multivariate Hermite polynomials of total Hermite degree \(j\). noindentStep 2: Moments of the chaos components. The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives sum_k_1,ldots,k_j=1^d big\|B^(a)_k_1,ldots,k_jbig\|_mathcal H^2 &le bigg( sum_r_1,ldots,r_a=1^d lambda_r_1^2cdotslambda_r_a^2 bigg) sum_k_1,ldots,k_j=1^d sum_r_1,ldots,r_a=1^d big\| T_r_1,r_1,ldots,r_a,r_a,k_1,ldots,k_j big\|_mathcal H^2 \\ &le \|Sigma\|_mathsf F^2a\|T\|_mathsf F^2. The Hermite orthogonality relations read \[ E mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft[ H_(k_1,ldots,k_j)(xi) H_(ell_1,ldots,ell_j)(xi) aftergroupegrouporiginalright] = sum_sigmain S_j prod_r=1^j 1_\k_r=ell_sigma(r)\, \] where \(S_j\) denotes the set of all permutations of \(\1,ldots,j\\). Since \(B^(a)_k_1,ldots,k_j\) is symmetric in \(k_1,ldots,k_j\), expanding \(E\|Y_j\|_mathcal H^2\) and applying these relations gives \[ mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft(E\|Y_j\|_mathcal H^2aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/2 = fracp!2^a a! j!sqrtj! bigg( sum_k_1,ldots,k_j=1^d lambda_k_1cdotslambda_k_j big\|B^(a)_k_1,ldots,k_jbig\|_mathcal H^2 bigg)^1/2 lesssim_p \|Sigma\|_mathsf F^a \|Sigma\|^j/2 \|T\|_mathsf F. \] Here we used the bound on \(B^(a)\) established above and \(lambda_kle\|Sigma\|\). The remaining prefactor is absorbed into the implicit constant since \(ale p/2\) and \(jle p\). Now let \(qge2\), set \(D:=dim(mathcal H)\), and let \(u_1,ldots,u_D\) be an orthonormal basis of \(mathcal H\). Each scalar projection \(langle Y_j,u_rrangle_mathcal H\) belongs to the \(j\)-th homogeneous Gaussian chaos. Therefore, Gaussian hypercontractivity gives mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| langle Y_j,u_rrangle_mathcal H aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q le (q-1)^j/2 mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| langle Y_j,u_rrangle_mathcal H aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_2. Hence, by the triangle inequality in \(L_q/2\), mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft(E\|Y_j\|_mathcal H^qaftergroupegrouporiginalright)^2/q &= bigg\| sum_r=1^Dbig|langle Y_j,u_rrangle_mathcal Hbig|^2 bigg\|_L_q/2 le sum_r=1^D big\|langle Y_j,u_rrangle_mathcal Hbig\|_L_q^2 le (q-1)^j\,E\|Y_j\|_mathcal H^2, and combining the two displays with \(a=(p-j)/2\) gives mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft(E\|Y_j\|_mathcal H^qaftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/q lesssim_p \|Sigma\|_mathsf F^(p-j)/2 \|Sigma\|^j/2q^j/2 \|T\|_mathsf F. noindentStep 3: Completion of the proof. Applying the triangle inequality to and using , we obtain \[ mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft(Ebig\|T(G_Sigma,ldots,G_Sigma)big\|_mathcal H^qaftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/q lesssim_p sum_substack0le jle p\jequiv p\!\!\!pmod2 \|Sigma\|_mathsf F^(p-j)/2 \|Sigma\|^j/2q^j/2 \|T\|_mathsf F = Psi_p(q,Sigma)\|T\|_mathsf F, \] which is the first estimate for \(qge2\). \label{def:stein}
Let \(Y\in\mathbb R^d\) be centered with
\(\mathbb{E}\|Y\|_2^2<\infty\). A measurable map
\[
\tau:\mathbb R^d\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d\times d}
\]
with $\mathbb{E}\|\tau(Y)\|_{\mathsf F}^2<\infty$
is called a \emph{Stein kernel} for \(Y\) if
\[
\mathbb{E}\langle Y,\varphi(Y)\rangle
=
\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
\tau(Y),\nabla\varphi(Y)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}
\]
for every smooth vector field
\(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) satisfying $\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft[
\|\varphi(Y)\|_2^2
+
\|\nabla\varphi(Y)\|_{\mathsf F}^2
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright]
<\infty$,
where
\[
\nabla\varphi
=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\frac{\partial\varphi_i}{\partial y_j}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)_{i,j=1}^d.
\]

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 1: A bounded Stein kernel for $Y$.}
\medskip

We first construct a bounded Stein kernel for \(Y\). Set
\[
\widetilde Y:=\Sigma^{-1/2}Y.
\]
The density of \(\widetilde Y\) is proportional to
\(\exp(-\widetilde V)\), where
\[
\widetilde V(y):=V(\Sigma^{1/2}y).
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation*}
\nabla^2\widetilde V(y)
=
\Sigma^{1/2}
\nabla^2V(\Sigma^{1/2}y)
\Sigma^{1/2}
\succeq
I_d.
\end{equation*}
Hence Fathi's bounded Stein-kernel result
\cite[Corollary~2.4]{fathi2019stein} yields a measurable symmetric
positive semi-definite Stein kernel \(\widetilde\tau\) for
\(\widetilde Y\) such that
\begin{equation}
0
\preceq
\widetilde\tau(\widetilde Y)
\preceq
I_d
\label{eq:ULC-whitened-Stein-order}
\end{equation}
almost surely.

Define
\begin{equation}
\tau(y)
:=
\Sigma^{1/2}
\widetilde\tau(\Sigma^{-1/2}y)
\Sigma^{1/2}.
\label{eq:ULC-Stein-transform}
\end{equation}
Then \(\tau\) is a Stein kernel for \(Y\). Indeed, let \(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) be a smooth vector
field satisfying the integrability condition in Definition \ref{def:stein},
and define
\[
\psi(y)
:=
\Sigma^{1/2}\varphi(\Sigma^{1/2}y).
\]
Since the change of variables is linear, \(\psi\) satisfies the
corresponding integrability condition under the law of
\(\widetilde Y\).
Since
\[
\nabla\psi(y)
=
\Sigma^{1/2}
\nabla\varphi(\Sigma^{1/2}y)
\Sigma^{1/2},
\]
the Stein identity for \(\widetilde Y\) gives
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\langle Y,\varphi(Y)\rangle
&=
\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
\widetilde Y,
\Sigma^{1/2}\varphi(\Sigma^{1/2}\widetilde Y)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle\\
&=
\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
\widetilde\tau(\widetilde Y),
\Sigma^{1/2}
\nabla\varphi(\Sigma^{1/2}\widetilde Y)
\Sigma^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}\\
&=
\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
\tau(Y),\nabla\varphi(Y)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}.
\end{align*}
Thus,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}\langle Y,\varphi(Y)\rangle
=
\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
\tau(Y),\nabla\varphi(Y)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}.
\label{eq:ULC-Stein}
\end{equation}
Furthermore, \eqref{eq:ULC-whitened-Stein-order} and
\eqref{eq:ULC-Stein-transform} imply
\begin{equation}
0
\preceq
\tau(Y)
\preceq
\Sigma
\label{eq:ULC-Stein-order}
\end{equation}
almost surely. Consequently, almost surely,
\begin{equation}
\|\tau(Y)\|
\le
\|\Sigma\|,
\qquad
\|\tau(Y)\|_{\mathsf F}
\le
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}.
\label{eq:ULC-Stein-norms}
\end{equation}















































































































Finally, the uniform convexity assumption implies that \(Y\) has moments
of every order. Indeed,
\[
V(y)
\ge
V(0)+\langle\nabla V(0),y\rangle
+\frac12\langle y,\Sigma^{-1}y\rangle,
\]
so the density of \(Y\) is bounded by a constant multiple of a shifted
Gaussian density. Hence every polynomial vector field, together with its
Jacobian, satisfies the integrability condition in Definition \ref{def:stein}. Therefore, \eqref{eq:ULC-Stein} applies to all polynomial
vector fields used below.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 2: A Hilbert-valued \(L_2\) estimate.}
\medskip

We prove the following stronger result. Set $\rho_0(\Sigma):=1$.
For every integer \(p\ge0\), every finite-dimensional real Hilbert space
\(\mathcal H\), and every \(p\)-linear map
\[
T:(\mathbb R^d)^p\longrightarrow\mathcal H,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ULC-Hilbert-bound}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}
\big\|
T(Y,\ldots,Y)
\big\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/2}
\le
C_p
\rho_p(\Sigma)
\|T\|_{\mathsf F},
\end{equation}
where \(C_p\) depends only on \(p\). For \(p=0\), a \(0\)-linear map is understood as a fixed vector in
\(\mathcal H\), and its Frobenius norm is its Hilbert-space norm.

Since symmetrizing \(T\) does not change \(T(Y,\ldots,Y)\) and cannot
increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\), we may assume without loss of generality
that \(T\) is symmetric. The case \(p=0\) is immediate with \(C_0=1\). For \(p=1\), applying
\eqref{eq:ULC-Stein} to linear vector fields gives
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(Y)
=
\mathbb{E}\tau(Y).
\]
Therefore, \eqref{eq:ULC-Stein-order} implies
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(Y)
\preceq
\Sigma.
\]
For every linear map \(T:\mathbb R^d\to\mathcal H\), it follows that
\[
\mathbb{E}\|T(Y)\|_{\mathcal H}^2
=
\mathrm{Tr}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
T\mathrm{Cov}(Y)T^*
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)
\le \mathrm{Tr}(T\Sigma T^*) \le
\|\Sigma\|
\mathrm{Tr}(TT^*)
=
\|\Sigma\|\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2.
\]
Since $\rho_1(\Sigma)=\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}$, then \eqref{eq:ULC-Hilbert-bound} holds for \(p=1\) with \(C_1=1\).

Fix \(p\ge2\), and suppose that
\eqref{eq:ULC-Hilbert-bound} holds through order \(p-1\) for every
finite-dimensional Hilbert space. Set
\[
P_T(y):=T(y,\ldots,y),
\qquad
f_T(y):=\|P_T(y)\|_{\mathcal H}^2,
\]
and write 
\[
m_p
:=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}\|P_T(Y)\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/2}.
\]
Since \(f_T\) is homogeneous of degree \(2p\), Euler's identity gives
\[
\langle y,\nabla f_T(y)\rangle
=
2p f_T(y).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb{E}\langle Y,\nabla f_T(Y)\rangle
=
2p\,\mathbb{E} f_T(Y)
=
2p m_p^2.
\]
Applying the Stein identity \eqref{eq:ULC-Stein} to the vector field $\varphi(y):=\nabla f_T(y)$, whose Jacobian is $\nabla\varphi(y)=\nabla^2f_T(y)$,
we obtain
\[
\mathbb{E}\langle Y,\nabla f_T(Y)\rangle
=
\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
\tau(Y),\nabla^2f_T(Y)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}.
\]
Combining the two identities yields
\begin{equation}
2p m_p^2
=
\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
\tau(Y),\nabla^2f_T(Y)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathsf F}.
\label{eq:ULC-Stein-polynomial}
\end{equation}

A direct differentiation gives
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial^2f_T}{\partial y_i\partial y_j}(y)
=
2p^2
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
T(y,\ldots,y,e_i),
T(y,\ldots,y,e_j)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathcal H}
+
2p(p-1)
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
P_T(y),
T(y,\ldots,y,e_i,e_j)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathcal H}.
\label{eq:ULC-Hessian}
\end{align}
Substituting \eqref{eq:ULC-Hessian} into

\mathbb{E}
\sum_{i,j=1}^d

\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle

\sum_{i,j=1}^d

\longrightarrow

\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(

\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)_{j=1}^d,

where \(\mathcal H^d\) is equipped with the product Hilbert-space norm

:=

Similarly, define the symmetric \((p-2)\)-linear map $\mathcal D_2T:

\longrightarrow

\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)_{i,j=1}^d,

:=
\sum_{i,j=1}^d\|h_{ij}\|_{\mathcal H}^2.

\begin{align*}

&=
\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_{p-1}=1}^d
\big\|
(\mathcal D_1T)(e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_{p-1}})

&=
\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_{p-1},j=1}^d

&=

\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_{p-2},i,j=1}^d
\big\|
T(e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_{p-2}},e_i,e_j)

=
\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2.
\end{align*}

\[
\|\mathcal D_1T\|_{\mathsf F}
=
\|\mathcal D_2T\|_{\mathsf F}
=
\|T\|_{\mathsf F}.
\]

\begin{align}
\bigg(
\mathbb{E}
\sum_{j=1}^d
\big\|
T(Y,\ldots,Y,e_j)
\big\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
&\le
C_{p-1}
\rho_{p-1}(\Sigma)
\|T\|_{\mathsf F},
\label{eq:ULC-first-derivative}\\
\bigg(
\mathbb{E}
\sum_{i,j=1}^d

T(Y,\ldots,Y,e_i,e_j)

&\le
C_{p-2}
\rho_{p-2}(\Sigma)

T(y,\ldots,y,e_i),

\begin{align*}

\le
p\|\Sigma\|
\mathbb{E}
\sum_{j=1}^d
\big\|
T(Y,\ldots,Y,e_j)

pC_{p-1}^2
\|\Sigma\|
\rho_{p-1}(\Sigma)^2
\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2.

\bigg(
\sum_{i,j=1}^d
\big\|
T(Y,\ldots,Y,e_i,e_j)

\nonumber\\
&\le
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}
\bigg(
\sum_{i,j=1}^d
\big\|
T(Y,\ldots,Y,e_i,e_j)

\begin{align*}
\circnum{2}&\le (p-1)\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft|
\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\langle
P_T(Y),
\sum_{i,j=1}^d
\tau_{ij}(Y)
T(Y,\ldots,Y,e_i,e_j)
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright|\\
&\le (p-1)
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}
\mathbb{E}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft[
\|P_T(Y)\|_{\mathcal H}
\bigg(
\sum_{i,j=1}^d
\big\|
T(Y,\ldots,Y,e_i,e_j)

\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(

\bigg(
\mathbb{E}
\sum_{i,j=1}^d
\big\|
T(Y,\ldots,Y,e_i,e_j)

&\le (p-1)
C_{p-2}
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}
\rho_{p-2}(\Sigma)
m_p
\|T\|_{\mathsf F},

\le
pC_{p-1}^2
\|\Sigma\|
\rho_{p-1}(\Sigma)^2
\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2
+
(p-1)C_{p-2}
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}
\rho_{p-2}(\Sigma)
m_p
\|T\|_{\mathsf F}.
\label{eq:ULC-moment-recursion}
\end{align}

\(\|\Sigma\|\le\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}\), implies
\[
\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}\rho_{p-1}(\Sigma)
\le
\rho_p(\Sigma),\qquad
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}\rho_{p-2}(\Sigma)

\rho_p(\Sigma).

Thus \eqref{eq:ULC-moment-recursion} yields
\[
m_p^2
\le
pC_{p-1}^2
\rho_p(\Sigma)^2
\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2
+
(p-1)C_{p-2}
\rho_p(\Sigma)
m_p
\|T\|_{\mathsf F}.

Since $t^2\le a^2+bt
$ implies $t\le a+b$ for $t,a,b\ge 0$,
we conclude that
\[
m_p
\le
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\sqrt p\,C_{p-1}
+
(p-1)C_{p-2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)
\rho_p(\Sigma)
\|T\|_{\mathsf F}.

The induction therefore closes upon setting

:=

+

By Frobenius duality, Cauchy--Schwarz, and \eqref{eq:ULC-Hilbert-bound} in \textbf{Step~2},

\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/2}

nodes.statement: Let \[ S:=sum_i=1^N Z_i, S':=sum_i=1^N Z_i', \] where \(Z_1',ldots,Z_N'\) is an independent copy of \(Z_1,ldots,Z_N\). Expanding the squared Hilbert-space norm gives \[ \|S\|_mathcal H^2 = sum_i=1^N\|Z_i\|_mathcal H^2 + sum_ine j langle Z_i,Z_jrangle_mathcal H. \] Therefore, \|S\|_L_q(mathcal H)^2 = mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\|\|S\|_H^2aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q/2 &le bigg\| sum_i=1^N\|Z_i\|_mathcal H^2 bigg\|_L_q/2 + bigg\| sum_ine j langle Z_i,Z_jrangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2\\ &= mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| bigg( sum_i=1^N\|Z_i\|_mathcal H^2 bigg)^1/2 aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q^2 + bigg\| sum_ine j langle Z_i,Z_jrangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2. Applying the Hilbert-space decoupling inequality with \(a_ij=1\) for all \(i,j\) and the convex function \(F(t)=|t|^q/2\), and then taking both sides to the power \(2/q\), we obtain \[ bigg\| sum_ine j langle Z_i,Z_jrangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2 le 4\, bigg\| sum_i,j=1^N langle Z_i,Z_j'rangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2 = 4\,\|langle S,S'rangle_mathcal H\|_L_q/2. \] On the event \(\Sne0\\), conditioning on \(S\) and using the independence of \(S\) and \(S'\), we have mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( EBig[ |langle S,S'rangle_mathcal H|^q/2 \,big| \, S Big] aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^2/q &= \|S\|_mathcal H mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( Emathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft[ mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft| bigglangle fracS\|S\|_mathcal H,S' biggrangle_mathcal H aftergroupegrouporiginalright|^q/2 \,middle|\, S aftergroupegrouporiginalright] aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^2/q\\ &le \|S\|_mathcal H sup_\|h\|_mathcal H=1 \|langle h,S'rangle_mathcal H\|_L_q/2. The same inequality is trivial on \(\S=0\\). Consequently, \|langle S,S'rangle_mathcal H\|_L_q/2 &le sup_\|h\|_mathcal H=1 bigg\| sum_i=1^N langle h,Z_i'rangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2 \|S\|_L_q/2(mathcal H)\\ &= sup_\|h\|_mathcal H=1 bigg\| sum_i=1^N langle h,Z_irangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2 \|S\|_L_q/2(mathcal H)\\ &le sup_\|h\|_mathcal H=1 bigg\| sum_i=1^N langle h,Z_irangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2 \|S\|_L_q(mathcal H). It follows that \|S\|_L_q(mathcal H)^2 le mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| bigg( sum_i=1^N \|Z_i\|_mathcal H^2 bigg)^1/2 aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q^2+ 4 sup_\|h\|_mathcal H=1 mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| sum_i=1^N langle h,Z_irangle_mathcal H aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q/2 \|S\|_L_q(mathcal H). Since \(t^2le a^2+4bt\) implies \(tle a+4b\) for t,a,bge 0, the upper bound follows. For the reverse inequality, let \(varepsilon_1,ldots,varepsilon_N\) be independent Rademacher random variables, independent of everything else. Since \[ Emathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft[ (Z_i-Z_i')_i=1^N \,middle|\, Z_1,ldots,Z_N aftergroupegrouporiginalright] = (Z_i)_i=1^N, \] conditional Jensen's inequality in \(ell_2^N(mathcal H)\) gives \[ mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| bigg( sum_i=1^N\|Z_i\|_mathcal H^2 bigg)^1/2 aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q le mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( E bigg( sum_i=1^N\|Z_i-Z_i'\|_mathcal H^2 bigg)^q/2 aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/q. \] For every fixed realization of \((Z_i,Z_i')_i=1^N\), Rademacher orthogonality and \(qge2\) imply bigg( sum_i=1^N\|Z_i-Z_i'\|_mathcal H^2 bigg)^q/2 = mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( E_varepsilon bigg\| sum_i=1^Nvarepsilon_i(Z_i-Z_i') bigg\|_mathcal H^2 aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^q/2le E_varepsilon bigg\| sum_i=1^Nvarepsilon_i(Z_i-Z_i') bigg\|_mathcal H^q. Consequently, mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| bigg( sum_i=1^N\|Z_i\|_mathcal H^2 bigg)^1/2 aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q &le mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft( E\,E_varepsilon bigg\| sum_i=1^Nvarepsilon_i(Z_i-Z_i') bigg\|_mathcal H^q aftergroupegrouporiginalright)^1/q= \|S-S'\|_L_q(mathcal H) le 2\|S\|_L_q(mathcal H). Here the equality follows because the random vectors \(Z_i-Z_i'\) are independent and symmetric. Moreover, for every \(hinmathcal H\) with \(\|h\|_mathcal H=1\), \[ bigg\| sum_i=1^Nlangle h,Z_irangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2 = \|langle h,Srangle_mathcal H\|_L_q/2 le \|langle h,Srangle_mathcal H\|_L_q le \|S\|_L_q(mathcal H). \] Therefore, \[ mathopenmathclosebgrouporiginalleft\| bigg( sum_i=1^N\|Z_i\|_mathcal H^2 bigg)^1/2 aftergroupegrouporiginalright\|_L_q + sup_\|h\|_mathcal H=1 bigg\| sum_i=1^Nlangle h,Z_irangle_mathcal H bigg\|_L_q/2 le 3\|S\|_L_q(mathcal H). \] Together with the upper bound, this completes the proof.

=
\sum_{i=1}^N\|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
+
\sum_{i\ne j}
\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle_{\mathcal H}.
\]
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
\|S\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}^2 = \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|\|S\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_{q/2}}
&\le
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N\|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}
+
\bigg\|
\sum_{i\ne j}
\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}\\
&=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N\|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}^2
+
\bigg\|
\sum_{i\ne j}
\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}.
\end{align*}
Applying the Hilbert-space decoupling inequality
\cite[Exercise~6.1.4]{vershynin2018high} with
\(a_{ij}=1\) for all \(i,j\) and the convex function
\(F(t)=|t|^{q/2}\), and then taking both sides to the power \(2/q\),
we obtain
\[
\bigg\|
\sum_{i\ne j}
\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}
\le
4\,
\bigg\|
\sum_{i,j=1}^N
\langle Z_i,Z_j'\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}
=
4\,\|\langle S,S'\rangle_{\mathcal H}\|_{L_{q/2}}.
\]
On the event \(\{S\ne0\}\), conditioning on \(S\) and using the
independence of \(S\) and \(S'\), we have
\begin{align*}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}\Big[
|\langle S,S'\rangle_{\mathcal H}|^{q/2}
\,\big| \,
S
\Big]
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{2/q}
&=
\|S\|_{\mathcal H}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft|
\bigg\langle
\frac{S}{\|S\|_{\mathcal H}},S'
\bigg\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright|^{q/2}
\,\middle|\,
S
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright]
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{2/q}\\
&\le
\|S\|_{\mathcal H}
\sup_{\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1}
\|\langle h,S'\rangle_{\mathcal H}\|_{L_{q/2}}.
\end{align*}
The same inequality is trivial on \(\{S=0\}\). Consequently,
\begin{align*}
\|\langle S,S'\rangle_{\mathcal H}\|_{L_{q/2}}
&\le
\sup_{\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1}
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N
\langle h,Z_i'\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}
\|S\|_{L_{q/2}(\mathcal H)}\\
&=
\sup_{\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1}
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N
\langle h,Z_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}
\|S\|_{L_{q/2}(\mathcal H)}\\
&\le
\sup_{\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1}
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N
\langle h,Z_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}
\|S\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}.
\end{align*}
It follows that
\begin{align*}
\|S\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}^2
\le
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N \|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}^2+
4
\sup_{\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\sum_{i=1}^N
\langle h,Z_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_{q/2}}
\|S\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}.
\end{align*}
Since \(t^2\le a^2+4bt\) implies \(t\le a+4b\) for $t,a,b\ge 0$, the upper bound
follows.

For the reverse inequality, let
\(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_N\) be independent Rademacher random
variables, independent of everything else. Since
\[
\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft[
(Z_i-Z_i')_{i=1}^N
\,\middle|\,
Z_1,\ldots,Z_N
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright]
=
(Z_i)_{i=1}^N,
\]
conditional Jensen's inequality in \(\ell_2^N(\mathcal H)\) gives
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N\|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}
\le
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N\|Z_i-Z_i'\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{q/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}.
\]
For every fixed realization of \((Z_i,Z_i')_{i=1}^N\), Rademacher
orthogonality and \(q\ge2\) imply
\begin{align*}
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N\|Z_i-Z_i'\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{q/2}
=
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N\varepsilon_i(Z_i-Z_i')
\bigg\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{q/2}\le
\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N\varepsilon_i(Z_i-Z_i')
\bigg\|_{\mathcal H}^q.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N\|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}
&\le
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbb{E}\,\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N\varepsilon_i(Z_i-Z_i')
\bigg\|_{\mathcal H}^q
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}=
\|S-S'\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}
\le
2\|S\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}.
\end{align*}
Here the equality follows because the random vectors
\(Z_i-Z_i'\) are independent and symmetric.

Moreover, for every \(h\in\mathcal H\) with \(\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1\),
\[
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N\langle h,Z_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}
=
\|\langle h,S\rangle_{\mathcal H}\|_{L_{q/2}}
\le
\|\langle h,S\rangle_{\mathcal H}\|_{L_q}
\le
\|S\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\|
\bigg(
\sum_{i=1}^N\|Z_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2
\bigg)^{1/2}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\|_{L_q}
+
\sup_{\|h\|_{\mathcal H}=1}
\bigg\|
\sum_{i=1}^N\langle h,Z_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}
\bigg\|_{L_{q/2}}
\le
3\|S\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)}.
\]
Together with the upper bound, this completes the proof.
